blocks.text: 1 Market Overview

blocks.html: US private equity recovered part of the ground it lost in the second quarter, but the recovery is narrow. 3Q26 deal value rose 20.9% QoQ to US$233.8bn and exit value rose 50.4% to US$165.5bn, yet year-to-date deal value is still 13.6% below last year and exit value 14.1% below. Two things carry the quarter: large exits to corporate buyers, with mega-exits at 73.3% of year-to-date exit value, and a rotation of capital out of software, where IT fell to 15.0% of deal value from 27.9% in 2025, into energy at 17.7%. Fundraising reached US$222.0bn across 348 funds, with funds under US$1bn taking only 16.6% of capital. The 25bp rate rise in September is the new variable for the fourth quarter. Our holding, Blue Owl GP Stakes V, had a positive quarter to 30 Jun 2026: GP portfolio value +1.4%, net IRR 7.8%, DPI unchanged at 0.4x.

2 Deal Activity
2.1 Deal value and count

blocks.html: Deployment rebounded from a weak second quarter without returning to last year's pace. 3Q26 deal value was US$233.8bn, up 20.9% from US$193.3bn in 2Q26 (restated) but 30.4% below the US$336.0bn of 3Q25, a quarter lifted by very large transactions. Deal count was 2,467, +5.9% QoQ and +7.9% YoY. For Q1–Q3, value is US$729.8bn (-13.6% YoY) on 7,189 deals (+6.0%): more transactions, smaller cheques. Large deals did return late in the quarter, with 28 transactions of US$1bn or more worth US$82.8bn, the largest at US$9.6bn.

blocks.text: 2.2 Deal composition

blocks.html: Add-ons still carry the buyout market at 74.9% of buyout count (74.0% in 2025) and 40.0% of buyout value. The median deal jumped to US$112.5m in 3Q26 from US$35.0m, and the average to US$675.2m from US$351.1m; one quarter of data, on the subset of deals with disclosed size, is a signal that larger platforms are trading again, not yet a trend. Secondary buyouts are 6.4% of buyout count year to date (6.0% in 2025) on PitchBook's restated series.

blocks.html: The sector mix has turned over within a year. Software deal value was US$17.7bn in 3Q26, 83.7% below the record US$108.5bn of 3Q25; Q1–Q3 software value is US$58.9bn, -62.8% YoY, while software deal count (184 in 3Q26) has fallen far less. IT is 15.0% of year-to-date disclosed deal value against 27.9% for 2025. Energy went the other way: US$117.7bn year to date, +105.1% YoY, and 17.7% of value against 7.1% in 2025. B2B remains the largest sector at 29.4%. Section 7.1 sets out why we read this as a rotation and not a pause.

blocks.text: 2.3 LBO volume in M&A context

blocks.html: Sponsors have lost share of a larger M&A market. Global M&A including estimates was US$1,021.1bn in 3Q26, -28.2% QoQ and -20.8% YoY, but Q1–Q3 value of US$4,084.2bn is still +22.6% YoY because the first half was driven by very large corporate transactions: deals above US$5bn were 52.3% of value in the first quarter, 42.9% in the second and 21% in the third. North America was US$532.0bn (-36.9% QoQ), US$2,435.2bn for Q1–Q3. On disclosed values, buyout/LBO is 31.8% of global M&A year to date against 41.6% in 2025, a fall of 9.8pp and the lowest share since 2016. Corporates with strong share prices set the marginal price this year; sponsors were outbid at the top of the market and were more active below it.

blocks.text: 2.4 Middle market

blocks.html: The middle market is where sponsor activity held up. 3Q26 middle-market deal value was US$90.4bn (+2.5% QoQ, -9.7% YoY) and deal count rose 24.1% QoQ to 1,124; Q1–Q3 value is US$277.9bn on 2,843 deals, -4.5% and +6.3% YoY. Its share of US buyout value recovered to 51.0% from 43.4% in 2025, when megadeals dominated. PitchBook attributes the preference for smaller transactions to financing costs after the September rate rise.

blocks.text: 2.5 How the volume measures nest — and where private credit connects

blocks.html: The volume figures in this report are successive cuts of one market. For Q1–Q3 2026: global M&A US$4,084.2bn; North America M&A US$2,435.2bn; US PE deal value US$729.8bn, which covers buyouts, add-ons and growth deals; US PE buyout/LBO US$586.6bn on disclosed values; and the US middle market, about US$299.0bn at 51% of buyout value.

blocks.html: Private credit meets this hierarchy on the financing side, at the buyout and middle-market layers. This quarter the syndicated loan market took business back: broadly syndicated loans refinanced a record US$11.8bn of direct-lending facilities in 3Q26 (US$2.2bn in 2Q26), while buyouts financed by private credit were largely absent at the large end and active in the lower middle market. Exhibit 12 maps each volume measure to its financing-side counterpart.

blocks.text: 3 Valuations, Performance & Financing
3.1 Entry multiples

blocks.html: Entry prices are lower than in 2025 on every broad measure, with thin samples. PitchBook no longer publishes the middle-market buyout multiple tables used in our previous issue, so Exhibits 13 and 16 now show buyouts of all sizes and Exhibit 15 a middle-market series from a different provider; none is comparable with the previous issue. The median North America and Europe buyout was done at 10.9x EV/EBITDA year to date (n=158) against 12.5x in 2025. The US middle-market median was 9.6x as of 31 Mar 2026 against 11.4x for 2025. US buyouts printed 12.0x EV/EBITDA on only n=46 (11.5x in 2025) and 2.1x EV/revenue (n=81; 2.4x in 2025); the EBITDA figure is indicative only. In the wider M&A market, global deals above US$5bn were priced at 13.6x (n=46), level with 2025, while US deals of US$25m–1bn rose to 11.4x from 9.8x (n=70): the discount for small size narrowed as buyers moved down-market.

blocks.text: 3.2 Fund performance: rolling horizon IRR

blocks.html: Fund returns are positive but low, and they lag: the latest reading is 4Q25 (as of 31 Dec 2025), about three quarters behind the deal data. The US rolling one-year IRR was 7.3% (8.0% a quarter earlier), with the middle market at 8.2% and megafunds at 6.5%. The middle market has been ahead of megafunds in each of the last three quarters shown. These figures predate both the software repricing of early 2026 and the third-quarter recovery in exits.

blocks.text: 4 Exits & Liquidity
4.1 Exit activity

blocks.html: Exit value recovered quickly, but through few doors. 3Q26 exits were US$165.5bn across 405 transactions, +50.4% QoQ and +54.4% YoY; Q1–Q3 exit value of US$428.1bn is still -14.1% YoY. Mega-exits of US$1bn or more account for 73.3% of the year's exit value. By route, sales to corporate acquirers were US$86.6bn of disclosed 3Q26 value, or 56.9%, sponsor-to-sponsor buyouts US$46.6bn and public listings US$19.0bn (-31.2% QoQ). The median disclosed exit is US$715.0m year to date (n=197) against US$500.0m in 2025: what sells is large and of high quality. The deals-to-exits ratio rose to 1.37 from 1.21, so the backlog is still building.

blocks.text: 4.2 Holding periods and inventory

blocks.html: The companies being sold are younger; the companies left behind are older. The median holding period of exited companies fell to 5.6 years year to date from 6.9 in 2025, while the median for companies still held rose to 4.2 years from 3.9. US sponsors hold 13,620 companies, of which 3,912 (28.7%) have been held six years or more and 1,522 (11.2%) nine years or more. GP-led secondaries remain the release valve for that older stock; the latest available figure is unchanged at US$22.5bn for the year to 30 May 2026, after US$98.2bn in 2025.

blocks.text: 5 Fundraising & Dry Powder
5.1 Fundraising

blocks.html: Fundraising is on course to fall short of 2025, and it is concentrated. US PE funds raised US$222.0bn across 348 funds in Q1–Q3, 67.3% of the US$329.9bn raised in 2025; a straight-line pace gives about US$296bn for the year. Funds under US$1bn took 16.6% of capital (18.2% in 2025). The average fund is US$674.9m against a median of US$48.1m, a ratio of 14 to one. Managers that do close are raising more than last time: the median step-up is 1.44x (1.36x in 2025).

blocks.text: 5.2 Dry powder and deployment runway

blocks.html: Dry powder rose because capital was raised faster than it was deployed. US PE dry powder was US$1,154bn as of 31 Mar 2026, +6.2% from the end of 2025; the middle market holds US$630bn, or 54.6%, and megafunds US$489bn. Middle-market buyout dry powder alone is a record US$493.8bn. Against trailing-four-quarter deal value of US$1,040.2bn, the runway is 1.11 years (0.94 for 2025). About one year of deal value is not an overhang: the pressure on sponsors comes from unsold companies, not from undeployed capital.

About one year of deal value is not an overhang: the pressure on sponsors comes from unsold companies, not from undeployed capital.

blocks.text: 7 Things We Should Know
7.1 The rotation from software to physical assets

blocks.html: Software was the largest single destination for buyout capital for a decade; in 2026 it is not. PitchBook's November note on “heavy assets, low obsolescence” (HALO) measures the move globally: software fell from 13.2% of PE deal value in 2025 to 9% through the third quarter, while energy, utilities and heavy industrials took a record 22.7%. Our US data agree: IT at 15.0% of deal value, energy at 17.7%. Three points follow. First, this is a repricing of obsolescence risk under AI, not a cyclical pause, so software volumes need not return to 2025 levels. Second, the destination is not cheap: the median HALO entry multiple rose from 7.2x to 9.6x between 2015 and 2025 and equity's share of the capital structure from 49.3% to 55.6%, which lowers leverage-driven returns. Third, exits lag: sponsors have closed more than four HALO deals for every exit since 2022, although HALO was 23% of global exit value this year against a five-year average of 18.3%.

7.2 A top-heavy recovery meets higher rates

blocks.html: The third-quarter rebound depended on a small number of large transactions and on corporate buyers. Mega-exits are 73.3% of year-to-date exit value, and corporate strategics drove nearly 60% of 3Q26 exit value; below that level the middle market's share of exit value is 28.9% and 28.7% of portfolio companies have been held six years or more. The 25bp rise in mid-September, with PitchBook expecting at least one more this year, raises the cost of exactly the large leveraged transactions that produced the rebound; the last tightening cycle cut megadeal activity sharply. We therefore treat 3Q26 as a recovery in price for the best assets, not yet as a recovery in liquidity for the average fund.

7.3 How the PE market impacts the private credit market

blocks.html: PE deal flow is the demand side of direct lending, and this quarter it sent three signals. Volume: buyout value of US$586.6bn for Q1–Q3 with a rising share of smaller deals means more, smaller loans; the lower middle market was the active pocket for direct lenders. Competition: the syndicated market refinanced a record US$11.8bn of direct loans in 3Q26, taking the larger and better credits and compressing spreads on what remains. Credit quality: an older inventory (4.2 years median for companies still held) and slow middle-market exits lengthen loan lives and raise the number of amend-and-extend requests ahead of the private credit maturity wall, while the sector rotation moves new lending from software to industrial and energy borrowers. Higher base rates support lender income but weaken interest coverage for those older borrowers. Readers should set this against the demand-side, CLO and spread sections of the Junson Private Credit Quarterly.

7.4 How the PE market impacts GP-stakes funds

blocks.html: A GP-stakes fund owns three things in its partner managers: fee income, a share of carry, and balance-sheet investments. Fee income depends on fundraising, and the pattern this quarter, with capital going to funds of US$1bn–5bn and to megafunds and step-ups at 1.44x, favours the established franchises such funds own; management fees were 25.4% of GPS V's cumulative gross distributions (23.4% a quarter earlier). Carry depends on exits, and exits are concentrated in a few large sales: carried interest was 27.7% of distributions and sale proceeds 7.8%, with DPI flat. Marks follow listed prices and fundraising outcomes more than deal flow: this quarter's two largest moves in GPS V were a listed share price (CVC, +11.5%) and a fundraising result (Bitkraft, -38.2%). The environment is supportive for fee streams, slow for carry and volatile for marks.

7.5 Implications for Junson

items: Hold GPS V; do not expect distributions to accelerate. Net IRR is 7.8% and DPI 0.4x, unchanged for four reporting periods. Value is accruing in marks (gross TVPI 1.6x) while cash waits on exits by partner managers.

For new PE commitments, favour the middle market and managers one size below the largest. That is where returns (8.2% against 6.5% for megafunds), deal share (51.0% of buyout value) and LP demand (52.7% of buyout fundraising) all point; the open issue is exits, at 28.9% of exit value.

Treat software exposure as a risk to be measured, not a growth assumption. Information technology is 8.5% of the underlying companies of GPS V's partner managers as printed in the latest letter; we will ask Blue Owl to confirm the figure, which is far below the previous letter's.

Read private credit and PE together. A record US$11.8bn of direct loans refinanced in the syndicated market in one quarter is a pricing signal for our credit holdings as much as a financing signal for sponsors.

blocks.html: Last quarter's thresholds. Not one of the three was met. Quarterly exit value was US$165.5bn, below US$200bn, and only one of the last four quarters exceeded that level. The deals-to-exits ratio is 1.37, not below 1.25. Funds under US$1bn took 16.6% of capital, not above 25%. The watch-list claim that IT would stay below 20% of deal value has held at 15.0%.

blocks.html: What would change our mind. We would turn more positive on liquidity if quarterly exit value exceeds US$200bn for two consecutive quarters with mega-exits a smaller share of it, if the deals-to-exits ratio falls below 1.25, or if funds under US$1bn take more than 25% of capital raised. We would turn more cautious if the buyout share of global M&A stays below 35% into next year, or if syndicated refinancing of direct loans stays above US$10bn a quarter while rates rise.

blocks.html: This update is based on Blue Owl's investor letter for 2Q26 (as of 30 Jun 2026), compared with the 1Q26 letter (as of 31 Mar 2026); the fund reports about two quarters behind this report. The quarter reversed part of the previous one: GP portfolio value rose 1.4% after falling 2.3% in 1Q26; LP net blended TVPI moved to 1.2x from 1.1x and net IRR to 7.8% from 7.6%, with DPI unchanged at 0.4x. Our assessment: “recovering marks, no new cash”.

blocks.html: Portfolio gross TVPI is 1.6x (1Q26: 1.5x) on paid-in cost of US$10,746.9m, with gross DPI at 0.4x.
